name: Russian Squat Routine
author: the Soviet weightlifting system, as passed on in English
structure: Six weeks for one lift. A recurring day of six sets of two at 80 %; on the other day the 80 % sets grow from three reps to six over three weeks, then become 5x5 at 85 %, 4x4 at 90 % and 3x3 at 95 %, ending with an attempt at 105 %.
progression: Fixed percentages of the starting max, reps first and intensity after. Nothing is adjusted inside the cycle; the test at the end sets the next one.
adapt: Sets, reps and percentages are laid out week by week; the app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Simple and effective, and leaves almost nothing over for other hard training. For the deadlift, start from a conservative max.

name: Smolov
author: Sergey Smolov
structure: Thirteen weeks of squatting: two introductory weeks, a four-week base cycle (4x9 at 70 %, 5x7 at 75 %, 7x5 at 80 %, 10x3 at 85 %), two transition weeks and a five-week intense cycle that ends in a max test.
progression: Fixed percentages with a set amount added to every day in the second and third base weeks, then a rest and a test. One or two easy weeks are needed afterwards.
adapt: Sets, reps and percentages change by day and week; the app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Known for large squat gains and for a high risk of injury and overtraining. Not for newer lifters, a calorie deficit or poor recovery.

name: Smolov Jr
author: adapted from Smolov
structure: Four days a week for three weeks on one lift: 6x6 at 70 %, 7x5 at 75 %, 8x4 at 80 %, 10x3 at 85 %.
progression: The same sets and reps each week with a set amount added in week two and again in week three, then an easy week and a test.
adapt: Loads are percentages of a max with fixed weekly additions; the app has no percentages and its own rule would decide the steps.
caveats: Used for a short push on the bench press or squat. Volume rises steeply and the joints feel it.

name: Sheiko #29-#32
author: Boris Sheiko
structure: Sixteen weeks in four blocks of high-volume, submaximal squat, bench press and deadlift, most of it at 68-80 % of a max: a preparatory block, the highest-volume block, a block rising to 85-90 %, and a peak with a taper.
progression: Every load is a percentage of the starting max and nothing is added from session to session. A test or a meet sets the max for the next cycle.
adapt: Every session's sets, reps and percentages are laid out for sixteen weeks; the app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Frequent benching and a great deal of technique practice. Sessions of 90-120 minutes and little deadlifting.

name: Bulgarian Method (powerlifting adaptation, Squat Every Day)
author: after Ivan Abadjiev; the powerlifting version written up by Greg Nuckols and others
structure: Squat and bench press worked up to the day's best clean single on most days of the week, with back-off sets as an option.
progression: The day decides the load; nothing is planned ahead. Volume comes down when performance keeps sliding.
adapt: The plan can hold the daily layout with progression off; the day's top single is the lifter's call and is not prescribed by the app.
caveats: The original was for full-time weightlifters. How long the adaptation can be kept up, and its injury risk, are disputed. The deload rules were not checked.

name: Coan-Phillipi Deadlift Routine
author: Ed Coan, for Mark Phillipi
structure: One deadlift day a week for ten weeks: a heavy set of two or three, several fast sets of three, then accessories.
progression: Percentages of a target max set above the current one, with high volume and short rests in weeks 1-6 and less volume at higher intensity in weeks 7-10.
adapt: Loads are percentages of a target max that change every week; the app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: A classic deadlift specialisation. A target set too high fails in the later weeks. Only the outline was checked.

name: Magnusson-Ortmayer Deadlift
author: Benedikt Magnusson, Travis Ortmayer
structure: One deadlift day a week: 4x4 at 70 %, a double at 80 % and one at 90 %, then a back-off set at 70 % for eight reps or more.
progression: When the back-off set reaches its rep target the working loads go up about 5 kg (10 lb) the next week; otherwise the week is repeated.
adapt: One session holds the same lift at three different percentages, and a planned exercise has one load for all its sets.
caveats: Covers the deadlift only; squat and bench need their own plan. Only the outline was checked.

name: Hepburn Method
author: Doug Hepburn
structure: Each lift twice a week. A strength part of eight sets of two at about 80 % of a max, working up to eight sets of three; optionally a pump part at 20 % less, from 3x6 to 3x8.
progression: Each session one more set goes from two reps to three. When all eight sets are threes, add 2.5-5 kg (5-10 lb) and start again at eight sets of two.
adapt: `double` over a range of two to three reps with eight sets raises the load once every set is a three, as the method does. Adding the reps one set at a time between those points is the lifter's part; the app does not pace it.
caveats: Slow and steady, for someone in no hurry. Only the outline was checked.

name: Candito 6 Week Strength Program
author: Jonnie Candito
structure: Six weeks, each with its own job: muscular conditioning, hypertrophy, a linear run to rep maxes, heavy acclimation and power, intense strength, then a deload and a test.
progression: Percentages of a max laid out for the block; the test in week six starts the next round.
adapt: Each week has different sets, reps and percentages; the app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Widely used. How many days each week trains was not checked week by week, nor the formula that turns an open set into a new max.

name: Calgary Barbell 16-Week
author: Bryce Krawczyk
structure: Squat three times a week, bench press four and deadlift three, through four phases: accumulation at 64-71 %, intensity at 76-82 % with a top set and back-off sets, meet preparation, and a taper into heavy triples and singles by RPE.
progression: Percentages rise week by week through the first three phases; in the last, top sets are chosen by RPE and back-off work shrinks. No deload week as such.
adapt: Percentages and RPE targets are laid out for sixteen weeks; the app has neither and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: One of the most used free peaking programmes. Sessions of 60-90 minutes, and it has to be run to the end.

name: TSA 9-Week Intermediate Approach
author: Bryce Lewis, The Strength Athlete
structure: Squat and deadlift twice a week each and bench press three or four times: four weeks of moderate-intensity volume, a deload in week five, three weeks of rising intensity, and a test or a meet in week nine.
progression: Main lifts by percentage of a max, with the top set corrected by RPE; rep targets differ between the days of a week.
adapt: Percentages and RPE targets are laid out for nine weeks; the app has neither and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Often used for a first meet. Only the outline was checked.

name: Juggernaut Method 2.0
author: Chad Wesley Smith
structure: Four four-week waves of tens, eights, fives and threes. Each wave: a week of several sets, a week with less volume at higher intensity, a week with one open set, a deload week.
progression: The working max after each wave rises by the reps beyond the standard on the open set, times a step (2.5 kg lower body, 1.25 kg upper body), counting at most ten reps.
adapt: Built on a working max recalculated every four weeks, with sets and reps that change weekly. The app has neither.
caveats: Submaximal, with room for size. Each lift is trained once a week, and it takes sixteen weeks to show.

name: Cube Method
author: Brandon Lilly
structure: Squat, bench press and deadlift each have their own day and rotate weekly through a heavy day, an explosive day and a rep day; a fourth day is bodybuilding-style work on weak points.
progression: Percentages of a max laid out for three three-week waves, load up and reps down from wave to wave, with a test in week ten.
adapt: Each lift's day changes its sets, reps and percentage every week; the app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: A simplified conjugate programme with the competition lifts themselves. Only the outline was checked.

name: Westside Barbell Conjugate
author: Louie Simmons
structure: Four days: lower-body max effort, upper-body max effort, lower-body dynamic effort, upper-body dynamic effort, with repetition-method accessories and conditioning around them.
progression: Max-effort days take one variation to a 1-3 rep max and change the variation often; dynamic-effort days move submaximal loads fast, usually in three-week waves. No fixed deload.
adapt: The max-effort exercise is replaced every one to three weeks, which would mean rewriting the plan that often, and the dynamic days run on percentages the app does not have.
caveats: Written for equipped powerlifting; how well it carries over to raw lifting is questioned. Only the outline was checked.

name: RTS / Emerging Strategies
author: Mike Tuchscherer, Reactive Training Systems
structure: The same training week repeated, loaded by RPE with volume set by a fatigue percentage, while the estimated max is logged week by week.
progression: The week repeats until the estimated max peaks and then falls; the number of weeks that took becomes the length of the lifter's next block, and a change of exercises takes the place of a deload.
adapt: Loads come from RPE and volume from a fatigue percentage; the app chooses neither.
caveats: Highly individual, and asks for a lot of honest logging. Only its existence and outline are confirmed; no original article was found.

name: DUP (Daily Undulating Periodization)
author: popularised by Michael Zourdos and others
structure: A way of laying out a week more than one programme: the same lift is trained on a hypertrophy day, a power day and a strength day, each with its own reps and intensity.
progression: Each day's rep range moves forward on its own. Published versions run on percentages that rise weekly and end in a test.
adapt: Put each day of a lift in its own routine: the app progresses a lift separately in each, which is what the layout asks for. The percentage tables of published versions are not available; each day runs on `linear` or `double` instead.
caveats: Stronger By Science considers it overrated as a method in itself. Only the outline was checked.

name: Hatch Squat Program
author: Gayle Hatch
structure: Two squat sessions a week for twelve weeks, each a descending pyramid of front squats and one of back squats.
progression: Percentages of a max rise week by week, ending with an attempt at 103 % in week eleven.
adapt: Each pyramid holds the lift at several percentages, and a planned exercise has one load for all its sets.
caveats: Suits weightlifters who need the front squat more than powerlifters. Only the outline was checked.
